clue.text: Business worked around inclusions, and yet with diligence

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

indicators.note: material that has been worked around has been kneaded and reshaped, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A firm has toiled away on added extras, and done it all carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: CO stays fixed at the front; only the letters of the next two words are shuffled to give the rest, CO + NSCIENTIOUSLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting conscientiously means taking great care and effort over a task, which is exactly working diligently.

clue.text: With nothing on there might be arrests, ok?

indicators.note: saying the result might be these letters signals that they are one possible rearrangement of what follows

parts.note: taken as written
K is text-message shorthand for okay

explanation.surface: A streaker is warned that appearing naked in public could get people arrested, all right?
explanation.walkthrough: Another reading: STARKERS with O (nothing) on top would be an anagram of ARRESTS OK, so the clue works either way. Starkers is British slang for completely naked.
explanation.definitionFit: Starkers is jokey British slang meaning stark naked, so a person wearing no clothes at all.

clue.text: Engineer rings to fasten on the wagon

indicators.note: fastening round something grips it, so one piece closes around the other

parts.note: a ring is shaped like the letter O, and there are two
someone on the wagon has stopped drinking, so is teetotal, TT

explanation.surface: An engineer is busy with rings for fixing something onto a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Os split, one on each side of TT. 'On the wagon' looks like a place for the fastening but is the idiom for giving up alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikolaus Otto was the German engineer who built the four-stroke internal combustion engine.

clue.text: A high point, the one of Akela's lads who goes the extra mile?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the highest hill in the Peak District of England

definitions.text: the one of Akela's lads who goes the extra mile?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read cryptically: of the boys in a pack, the more generous helper

explanation.surface: A proud moment for the cub pack: the boy who always does more than asked.
explanation.walkthrough: Akela is the leader of a Cub Scout pack, so her lads are scouts; one who goes the extra mile is a kinder scout. The question mark flags the playful second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinder Scout is a moorland plateau in Derbyshire, the summit of the Peak District, so a high point.

clue.text: Endure way hatred's taking the usual form

parts.note: to stand something is to endure it

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: an aversion is a strong dislike
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Putting up with a road's hostility has become the normal state of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' wants to be a manner of doing things; it is the road abbreviation, and it lands just after the first letter of the hatred word.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard version is the regular, default edition of something, the ordinary form it usually takes.

clue.text: A cosmetic crack

parts.note: a means one
liner, as in eyeliner, is a cosmetic

explanation.surface: A crack in make-up, or a gap in a beauty product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' reads as a split, but here it is a wisecrack, a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisecrack is a quick witty remark, and a one-liner is a joke delivered in a single sentence.

clue.text: See 22
See 13
Hit Head of Technology with one project to keep peace!

indicators.note: keeping something means holding on to it, so one piece holds another inside
the head of a word is its top, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter
W is the abbreviation for with
the Roman numeral for one
to stand out is to project or stick out
sh is the call for quiet, peace

explanation.surface: A tech chief is struck while running a peacekeeping scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' looks like a verb acting on the head of technology, but it is the definition: a hit record. 'Peace' is the shushing call for quiet, which splits the two-word verb for project.
explanation.definitionFit: Twist and Shout is a 1960s song made famous by the Beatles, a chart success, so a hit.

clue.text: To right of Caliban expert conceals opening on stage

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: an ace is an expert
taken as written

indicators.note: the right-hand side of a written word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: An authority on Shakespeare's monster hides something at the start of a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Caliban is the monster in The Tempest, which tempts you to look for the answer in the play; only his last letter is used. Ace for expert is everyday slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The first act of a play is how a stage performance begins, its opening section.

clue.text: Typical method by which one exploits agent of pest control

parts.note: MO, modus operandi, is a usual way of working
a user is one who exploits others

explanation.surface: Describing the standard technique an exterminator uses on vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: MO stands for modus operandi, Latin for a way of operating.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouser is a cat kept for catching mice, a living form of rodent control.

clue.text: Maybe the second row's not written about

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: something oral is spoken rather than written
a row, rhyming with cow, is a noisy quarrel, a din

explanation.surface: Perhaps the second line of a table has gone unrecorded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts as a line of seats or figures, but it is the rhymes-with-cow sense, a racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Second is an example of an ordinal number, one that gives position in a sequence, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Press grasping furniture store after review to snap up deal

indicators.note: grasping means clutching in the hand, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to strain is to press hard or push
IKEA is the Swedish flat-pack furniture retailer

indicators.note: a review looks back over things, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: to grab is to snap up eagerly

explanation.surface: The press covers a furniture shop whose sale lets shoppers grab a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' reads as journalists, but it is a verb meaning push hard, and that word splits open to take in the Swedish shop and the turned-round snatch.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal is to do business, and striking a bargain means agreeing terms in a trade, so the verb phrase fits.

clue.text: Order two pints in the end: Burton Ale

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, here into a fresh sequence

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: At closing time, someone asks for two pints of Burton beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Burton upon Trent is a famous English brewing town, which makes 'Burton Ale' look like one name, but Burton is anagram fodder and Ale is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown stout is an old style of dark, strong beer, broadly a kind of ale.

clue.text: I refuse to live over literary wood

indicators.note: turning over flips something end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: saying no is refusing
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: Someone declines to live beneath a forest from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary' warns that the word is poetic: it is the old form of ebony.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebon is a poetic, archaic word for ebony, the hard black timber, so a wood found in literature.

clue.text: Couples in bar neck chianti — what impertinence!

indicators.note: a couple is a pair, so only two letters are kept from each of the following words

parts.note: first two letters, the opening couple
last two letters
first two letters, the opening couple
last two letters

explanation.surface: Pairs of lovers in a pub swig wine, and someone tuts at their cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: The pairs alternate between the front and back of each word. 'What' looks like part of the exclamation but supplies the last two letters, leaving 'impertinence' as the definition. 'Neck' is British slang for drinking quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Backchat is British slang for cheeky answering back, rude replies that show a lack of respect.

clue.text: See 4
Such a cat might be a man

definitions.text: Such a cat might be a man

parts.words: Such a cat might be a man
parts.note: surface reading: a puzzling claim that some cat could be a human

parts.words: Such a cat might be a man
parts.note: setter's reading: a Manx cat, docked of its final letter, becomes MAN

explanation.walkthrough: Manx cats, from the Isle of Man, are born without tails; take the tail letter off MANX and you have MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manx breed is famous for having no tail, so the description fits that cat exactly.

clue.text: DeGeneres the voice of her party line

parts.note: a do is a party
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: The comedian Ellen DeGeneres speaking for her political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party line' looks like a political phrase, but party and line are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen DeGeneres voiced Dory, the forgetful blue fish in the Pixar film Finding Nemo.

clue.text: Divers in SOS: aides probing subject of inquiry — this?

definitions.text: Divers in SOS: aides probing subject of inquiry — this?

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: a case is a matter under investigation

indicators.note: divers means various or assorted, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Divers in trouble send a distress call while helpers investigate the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: divers who surface too fast get this condition. 'Divers' is both the anagram signal and the people at risk.
explanation.definitionFit: Caisson disease is decompression sickness, the bends, which divers suffer when rising too quickly from depth.

clue.text: It's regrettable about your escalating wage

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: alas is the cry for something regrettable

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters are backwards

parts.note: YR is the abbreviation for your

explanation.surface: Someone is sorry to hear that your pay keeps rising.
explanation.walkthrough: Each piece is turned round separately, and they stay in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: A salary is fixed regular pay for work, and wage is a near synonym for earnings.

clue.text: See 8
Eucalyptus to ground, our highest faller

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed and broken up, so these letters are reformed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gum tree brought down to earth is the tallest thing in the country to topple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faller' sounds like a felled tree, but it is something that falls continuously: a waterfall. 'Our' means England's.
explanation.definitionFit: Cautley Spout in the Howgill Fells, Cumbria, is England's highest cascade waterfall above ground.

clue.text: East side of city on Dee, Aberdeen's over there

indicators.note: east is the right-hand side on a map, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter
taken as written
dee is the spelt-out name of the letter D

explanation.surface: Aberdeen sits on the River Dee, and someone points across the city.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdeen really is on the River Dee, which makes 'Dee' look like the river, but it is the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: Yond is a Scots and archaic word meaning yonder, at that distant place, as an Aberdonian might say.

clue.text: Capital letter indicating new driver is attached to rear of cab first

indicators.note: first tells you to put the following piece in front, ahead of the one just named

parts.note: UK learner drivers display an L plate
taken as written

indicators.note: the rear of anything is its back end, so only the final character is kept

parts.note: last letter
on means attached to, as a button on a coat

explanation.surface: A capital L shows a new driver, with a plate stuck on the back of a taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital letter' reads as an upper-case letter; split it, and Capital is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisbon is the capital city of Portugal, the seat of its government.

clue.text: See 9
I run 180m downhill and consult our doctors

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are altered in order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fell runner sprints down a slope and then sees the team medics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like a noun after 'our', but it is a verb meaning tampers with. The speaking 'I' is the waterfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Cauldron Snout is a cascade on the River Tees about 180 metres long, water that runs down a hillside.
